extracted.intended_audience: Victorian English readers of lectures/essays (educated gentlemen and ladies interested in social reform and moral instruction)
extracted.subtask_description: A Victorian lecture/essay giving prescriptive guidance on civic duty, charity, education, housing, and the arts — instructing readers how to act and what reforms to pursue. The text prescribes priorities and practical actions for individuals and the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three first needs of civilized life
rubrics_metrics.description: Feeding people, dressing people, and lodging people are the first and primary needs of civilized life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states these explicitly as the three first needs and insists that every Christian man and woman should be in direct service toward one of these needs (as far as consistent with their occupation), or wholly so if they have no special business. Outlines an order of priority: feed first, then clothe, then lodge, and claims that out of such plain duty all other good will come.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feed the hungry (indiscriminate charity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral obligation is to feed the hungry — not only the 'deserving' or industrious, but simply to feed the hungry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects selective 'indiscriminate charity' rhetoric; insists on organization of agriculture and commerce to produce wholesome food, proper storing and distribution so famine is impossible. Practical measure: ensure there is food to give before enforcing standards; handle vagrancy by identifying and sequestering vagabonds so honest people are not starved with them, and require work from those sequestered ('if any man will not work, neither should he eat') — but priority remains availability of food to give.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dress people: promote cleanliness and consistent dress
rubrics_metrics.description: Urge everyone within influence to be neat and clean and provide them the means to be so; prefer adoption of a consistent dress for different ranks and restriction of rapid fashion changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage and support those willing to dress with propriety; accept that some will refuse and stop exertion toward them but protect children and willing people from being brought up in squalor. Views conquest of vanity and frivolity as necessary to make consistent dress possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lodge people: housing reform and sanitary action
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide decent lodging via legislation and remedial sanitary action; build durable, beautiful grouped housing with gardens and belts of fresh air so no festering suburbs exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires cutting down vested interests, immediate remedial work (mend roofs, fix fences, prop floors, buttress walls), and long-term planning: houses kept in proportion to streams, walled groups, surrounding gardens and orchards so fresh air and open country are a short walk away. Immediate practical action (hands-on cleaning) is commended as useful and instructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical religion: faith founded on helpful action
rubrics_metrics.description: True religion must be daily founded on rational, effective, humble, and helpful action rather than on meditative differences of creed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against dwelling on points of difference with others (the Pharisee's sin). When people find common practical good to do, they should do it together: joint action prevents quarrelling. Criticizes religious enthusiasm divorced from daily useful duties (e.g., women steeped in vain meditation instead of learning sewing, cooking, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Education must be practical and serviceable
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should teach practical skills (sewing, cooking, accounting, basic medicine, agricultural and building skills) and make people useful, not merely ornamental accomplishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that many girls and youths lack simple useful skills; giving them true work will turn wasted enthusiasm into beneficent peace. Competitive examinations become wholesome only when they are calm, daily, and in practice. Practical arts and serviceable knowledges will sustain greater arts and theoretical sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do the work of men: active moral engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: While alive, people must 'do the work of men' — act boldly, usefully, and ethically, not live passively or as mere pleasure-seekers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if life is short or there is no afterlife, one should live nobly and perform manly work. The excuse 'cannot leave my station in life' is often a cover for selfish maintenance of comforts; those who truly cannot should still do their work honestly. Readiness to leave station when duty requires (as apostles did) is commended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frugality and sacrifice for public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals should live on as little as they can, do wholesome work, and spend spare resources on doing 'sure good' for others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal sacrificial living and active giving are framed as preconditions of meaningful social reform — people must reduce personal consumption to enable effective charity and public action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts and culture should follow healthy practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The fine arts will healthily follow from direct, holy, and simple practical practice; cultural excellence is a corollary of social and material well-being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that through direct contention with material evil people will discover truths and supports for higher arts; thus social reform precedes and nourishes artistic flourishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban planning: grouped housing with access to fresh air
rubrics_metrics.description: Cities should be planned with grouped housing, limited extent, proportionate to water streams, walled where appropriate, and surrounded by belts of gardens and orchards to ensure fresh air and horizon access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term aim: no festering suburbs, but clean busy streets and open country within a few minutes' walk. This is paired with immediate sanitary repairs and enforcement of cleanliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building as the enduring art
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of building is the most durable and accumulative human art; well-made buildings can outlast and better withstand natural forces than ephemeral works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complains that much ancient skill leaves no vestige but fallen stones; urges constructive, progressive building that provides civic pride, defence, habitation, and permanent record of human power and care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weaving and clothing as essential craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Weaving and clothing ought to clothe people well; the author condemns the current state where centuries of weaving still leave many poorly clothed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticizes industrial production that yields cast clouts and rotten rags; suggests that arts of spinning and weaving should contribute to universal decent clothing rather than cheap, shameful garments.

rubrics_metrics.name: The state as the nation’s almoner
rubrics_metrics.description: Dispensers of poor-rates (state relief) ought to act as national almoners, distributing alms with gentleness and freedom beyond what individual charity could achieve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that state distribution should be kinder and freer, based on collective wisdom and power rather than the stinginess or moralism of private charity; this principle is foundational for laws about pauperism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public education as the cure for public distress
rubrics_metrics.description: The only true cure for public distress is public education directed to make men thoughtful, merciful, and just.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws can only help gradually and depend on national temper improvement; public education is a prerequisite for making other reforms effective and for strengthening national character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical engagement reveals the nature of evil
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct contention with material evil (through service) is the way to understand what is actually wrong in society and to discover unexpected helps and truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speculation alone will not raise the practical truths that service and work will; by doing, people will find solutions to educational and social problems that theory cannot provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act as if under daily moral judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: One should live under the sense that judgment is present daily — conduct life with accountability now, not only at some future Last Judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asserts 'every day is a Dies Iræ' and that judgment waits at doors and corners — the elements, the oppressed, and the moments wasted serve as judges. This is an imperative for immediate moral responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conquer vanity and luxury to enable reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Social reforms (like consistent dress and reduced waste) require overcoming personal vanity, frivolity, and the desire to appear what one is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques the consumption of luxuries and translated (secondhand/imported) dress; reducing these vices is necessary to make practical reforms feasible and honest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivated elites owe duties in return for privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: The production of 'highly-bred' cultured persons involves sacrifice by many; such cultivated people therefore have duties of living service in return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges the value of producing refined human beings but insists they must perform duties ('living belfry and rampart') and not live merely on the contributed life of others.
